name: The Deadly Mantis
description: A prehistoric praying mantis thawed from the Arctic ice and heading south

film.title: The Deadly Mantis
film.star: A giant mechanical model, with no actor inside
film.note: Premiered in Los Angeles on 1 May 1957 and went out across America later that month on a double bill with the spy film The Girl in the Kremlin. Produced by William Alland, who also made Creature from the Black Lagoon.

legend: The Deadly Mantis is Cold War anxiety with antennae. A volcanic eruption in the South Seas shifts the polar ice, and out of it crawls a praying mantis bigger than a bomber, frozen since prehistoric times. It wipes out a radar station on the Distant Early Warning Line, the chain of Arctic stations built to spot Soviet bombers, then flies south over Canada and down the eastern seaboard with the Air Force in pursuit. Craig Stevens plays the colonel who tracks it, William Hopper the palaeontologist who identifies it, and the trail ends in the Manhattan Tunnel, where the creature is finished off with gas bombs. The film leans heavily on real military footage, and its long tour of radar fences and scrambling jets is as much a recruiting film as a monster movie, which is part of its charm.

myths.claim: The mantis was created by atomic testing.
myths.explanation: It's a prehistoric survivor, freed from the Arctic ice when a volcanic eruption on the other side of the world shifts the polar cap.

myths.claim: The mantis dies in a New York road tunnel.
myths.explanation: The finale takes place in the Manhattan Tunnel, where the colonel's team goes in with gas bombs to finish it off.

myths.claim: The Deadly Mantis was shot in colour.
myths.explanation: It's black and white, which helped the real military stock footage blend in with the new scenes.

myths.claim: Much of the film is real Air Force footage.
myths.explanation: Universal padded the story with genuine footage of radar stations, scrambling jets and Arctic bases.

powers: Flight at the speed of a jet
weaknesses: Being the only one of its kind
legacy: Mystery Science Theater 3000 riffed on it in 1997
Giant mantises returned in Son of Godzilla (1967) as the Kamacuras
Its story came from producer William Alland, who had given Universal Creature from the Black Lagoon
facts: The mantis is freed from the Arctic ice after a volcano erupts in the South Seas
Its first victims are the crew of a Distant Early Warning radar station in the Arctic
It flies south from the Arctic to Washington, D.C. and New York
The finale takes place in the Manhattan Tunnel, where it is killed with gas bombs
Much of the film is real Air Force footage of radar stations and jets
It was released on a double bill with the spy film The Girl in the Kremlin
Star Craig Stevens went on to play television's Peter Gunn the following year
hostIntro: Tonight's guest has been in the freezer since before the dinosaurs went out of fashion. Now she's thawed, she's hungry, and she's heading for the city. Don't bother praying; she's better at it.
